Ten to one. A few drops of tea tree oil to roughly ten times as much carrier oil (coconut, jojoba, or almond). That ratio is what keeps it working without torching your skin.

Patch test first. Dab the diluted mix on your inner forearm, wait 24 hours, see how your skin reacts. Cheaper to learn that way than on your face.

You've already got the base that works, almond milk plus vanilla plus honey. Don't rewrite it. Two variations worth trying this week, both drop the sugar load without losing the body:

**Date and cinnamon.** One cup almond milk, one pitted Medjool date, half a teaspoon cinnamon, pinch of salt. Blend 30 seconds. The date does the sweetening and adds thickness honey can't, and it doesn't taste like a compromise.

Keeps five days in the fridge, shake before you pour.

expect: The user would prefer responses that acknowledge and build upon their existing efforts to organize their kitchen, such as utilizing their new utensil holder to keep countertops clutter-free. They would also appreciate tips that address their concern for maintaining their granite surface, particularly around the sink area. Preferred responses would provide practical and actionable steps to maintain cleanliness, leveraging the user's current tools and setup. They might not prefer generic or vague suggestions that do not take into account their specific kitchen setup or concerns.
pred:
Kitchen mess is never a motivation problem. It's a friction problem. Design it out.

Three things, in order of impact. First, cut the number of decisions. Everything that has a home gets put away without thinking: one drawer for utensils, one spot for the cutting board, one bin for recycling. When a thing has no home, it lands on the counter forever. Second, kill the pile at the source. Clean as you cook, not after. The pan gets scrubbed while the sauce simmers, ten seconds each, versus a forty minute pile at 9pm when you'd rather be doing anything else. Third, keep the surface clear as a hard rule. Empty counter equals room to work, and room to work means the mess never compounds.

Then run the smallest possible nightly loop: dishes, wipe the counter, take the trash out. Five minutes. Same time every night, before you sit down.

Do that for a week and watch whether it holds. If some spot still piles up, that's your real signal, not laziness. Something there is missing a home. Tell me which spot keeps breaking and we'll fix that one specifically.

expect: The user would prefer responses that provide tips and advice specifically tailored to their slow cooker experiences, utilizing their recent success with beef stew and interest in making yogurt in the slow cooker. They might not prefer general slow cooker recipes or advice unrelated to their specific experiences and interests.
pred:
Slow cookers are simple machines, which is exactly why most disappointing results come down to two variables you can actually measure: temperature and moisture. Everything else is noise. Here's how I'd debug it.

First, verify the machine. Fill your slow cooker two-thirds with water, set it to low, and check the water temp after four hours with an instant-read thermometer. Low should land somewhere around 190 to 200 F and hold there. Plenty of cheap cookers overshoot into a rolling simmer, which is what turns chicken stringy and vegetables to mush. If yours runs hot, cook on the warm setting or use a timer that cuts the power early. Warm should sit around 165 to 175 F, which is actually fine for most braises if you give it more time.

Second, cut your pieces bigger than feels right. Root vegetables at two inches, meat in three-inch chunks. Small pieces surrender all texture by hour three.

Third, layer with intent. Root vegetables and aromatics on the bottom, where the heat is, meat above. Never fill past two-thirds, and add liquid only to about a third of the way up the food. Slow cookers make their own liquid, and swimming vegetables steam instead of caramelize.

Fourth, sear meat and bloom spices in a pan first if you care about flavor depth. It costs ten minutes and buys back most of what the slow cooker takes away.

Fifth, leave the lid alone. Every peek dumps twenty minutes of accumulated heat, and the recovery costs you texture.

Last, thicken and season at the end, not the start. Salt early pulls moisture out of everything. A slurry of cornstarch or a knob of butter stirred in during the final ten minutes does more than any recipe tweak.

What specifically is going wrong? Dry meat, bland liquid, mushy vegetables, or something burning at the edges? Tell me which and I'll get surgical. Tuning beats guessing, and soup doesn't need another rewrite.
